antibody, and found that GFP is expressed in kidneys injected with AAV9-Cbh-EGFP and AAV9-
Ksp-EGFP but not that in kidneys injected with blank AAV (new Extended Data Fig. 8), confirming
the specificity of AAV-mediated GFP expression in kidneys.
Even in the study cited by the authors, AAV9 transduction was largely restricted to mesangial cells within
the glomeruli, with only minimal transduction in proximal tubule cells (~9% efficiency) and higher
expression in podocytes. The investigator utilized the split-base editor system to express the base editor
(due to size limitation). This requires the same cell to be transduced simultaneously by two different
AAV9 viruses for the system to work, which will further reduce the editing. To validate transduction
efficiency, vector genome and vector genome transcript levels should be quantified in various organs.
Additionally, measuring AAV copy number in the liver and kidney is crucial to assess how long the base
editor remains active and whether immune clearance affects AAV persistence over time. The stability or
decline of AAV expression over time should also be addressed. If AAV expression levels are
disproportionately high, the observed effects may not be due to successful base editing alone but could
instead result from AAV overload, potentially affecting cellular functions in unintended ways. The
authors should clarify whether their findings are influenced by non-specific AAV effects rather than
precise gene editing.
Response: Thanks for your comments and suggestions. We address these concerns point-by-
point below:
1) To validate transduction efficiency, vector genome and vector genome transcript levels should be
quantified in various organs.
Response: We have evaluated the transduction efficiency of Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and Ksp-
ABE9-dual-AAV9 in the kidney, liver, and heart by examining the levels of Cas9 protein in those
organs. In addition, we also detected the Cas9 mRNA level in the kidneys, livers, and hearts from
3- and 6-month-old Pkd1RC/RC mice after injected with Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9. The new results
showed that the expression of Cas9 protein level could be detected in kidneys, livers and hearts
in Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 injected Pkd1RC/RC mice, and the expression of Cas9 could mainly be
detected in kidneys and livers in Pkd1RC/RC mice treated with Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 (new
Extended Data Fig. 21a-21d). Furthermore, both protein and mRNA level of Cas9 are decreased
in the kidneys, livers, and hearts from 6-month-old Pkd1RC/RC mice.
2) measuring AAV copy number in the liver and kidney is crucial to assess how long the base editor remains
active and whether immune clearance affects AAV persistence over time.
Response: Thanks for your comments and suggestions. We have cited the papers which showed
the duration of AAV in the liver and kidney (PMID: 29599079). In addition, to validate transduction
efficiency of Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 particles in vivo, we found that
Cas9 protein and mRNA could be detected in kidneys, livers and hearts in Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9
injected Pkd1RC/RC mice, and Cas9 protein could mainly be detected in kidneys and livers in Ksp-
ABE9-dual-AAV9 injected Pkd1RC/RC mice (Extended Data Fig. 21a-21d). In addition, we found
that there was a significant reduction of the AAV copy number and Cas9 expression over time in
6-month Pkd1RC/RC mice kidneys and livers after post-injection with Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9
(Extended Data Fig. 21e and 21f). The transient expression of Cas9 following AAV delivery
supports a “hit-and-go” gene editing model, in which Cas9 is briefly expressed to introduce the
desired genomic changes and then cleared gradually, thereby minimizing long-term Cas9
exposure and associated risks. Depending on the route of administration, choice of serotype and
dosage used, the general AAVs (including AAV9) exhibits a relatively tolerable safety profile when
compared to other gene transfer devices like adenovirus (Ad) and lentivirus (PMID: 33837614).
We have also revised the discussion section as that “AAVs are favored for their safety, low
immunogenicity, and ability to provide long-lasting gene expressions, which are particularly useful
for targeting non-dividing cells, such as those in the heart, kidney and liver (PMCID: PMC9418752,
PMCID: PMC12272985, PMCID: PMC3799231). A number of theories have been proposed to
explain the relatively low immunogenicity of AAV. First, most AAV serotypes may be poor
transducers of professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs), such as dendritic cells, and may only
result in minimal upregulation of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) proteins, key molecular
players in the presentation of antigens to the immune system, in target cell types. Second, there
is a balance between immune tolerance and the clearance of AAV-delivered components (e.g.,
Cas9) after AAVs treatment. High dosage of AAV is easy to activate T cells to induce the immune
clearance of AAV, resulting in the loss of efficacy, but low dose is more likely to be neutralized by
anti-AAV antibodies (PMID: 36635967). However, in some contexts, moderate doses may
promote immune tolerance, rather than immune activation, particularly in immune-modulatory
organs, such as the liver. Certain degree of base editing vector uptake/accumulation and the
expression of base editor is inevitable in livers, even with tissue-enriched promoters. This is a
known limitation of AAV9 delivery and does not necessarily reflect promoter leakiness but rather
a vector biodistribution.”
In our study, we observed that although the copy number of AAV vector in the kidney and liver
decreased over time, the base editing efficiency remained stable. This suggests that the AAV
levels of base editor during the early post-injection window was sufficient to induce durable and
irreversible genomic editing. Such a phenomenon is consistent with the mechanism of base
editing, where even short-term expression of the editor can result in permanent genetic correction
(PMCID: PMC12284509). Therefore, while immune clearance may reduce AAV vector
persistency, it does not necessarily compromise therapeutic efficacy, providing that sufficient
editing occurs before vector elimination.
3) The stability or decline of AAV expression over time should also be addressed.
Response: Thanks for your suggestion. We have revised the discussion section as that “The
stability of AAV mediated base editor expression can be influenced by several factors, including
the specific serotype, the target tissue, specific promoters, and the route of administration (PMID:
9156805; PMID: 18414476). It has been reported that AAV vector-mediated the expression of the
transgene is generally maintained in vivo for at least 6 months (PMCID: PMC9702554). In
essence, the initial burst of AAV gene delivery, possibly resulting in a higher copy number, and
the stability of episomal genomes in non-dividing cells and the potential for low-level integration,
can collectively contribute to the observed long-term maintenance of transgene expression
despite a decline in the overall AAV copy number over time (PMCID: PMC9077371). As such,
copy number and transgene expression are not always directly proportional. In our study, we
observed a decline in AAV vector copy number and Cas9 protein expression over time in the heat,
kidney and liver, whereas the base editing efficiency remained stable, which is consistent with the
mechanism of base editing that even short-term expression of the editor can result in permanent
genetic correction (PMID: 40704025). These results suggest that the subsequent declines in AAV
copy number and Cas9 expression do not negate those already established genomic changes,
which supports a “hit-and-go” editing model that minimizes long-term exposure to the editing
machinery. This concept is crucial for the development of safe and effective long-term gene
therapies using CRISPR-Cas9 delivered via AAV vectors (PMCID: PMC9077371, PMCID:
PMC110396, PMID: 12946324).”
4) The authors should clarify whether their findings are influenced by non-specific AAV effects rather than
precise gene editing.
Response: Thanks for your comments. To clarify whether the observed phenotypic changes were
caused by precise gene editing rather than non-specific effects of AAV delivery or transgene
expression, we treated Pkd1RC/RC and Pkd1RC/null mice with AAVs carrying a non-targeting sgRNA
that does not recognize any genomic locus. This non-targeting sgRNA control allowed us to
evaluate the effects arising from viral infection, vector expression, or dCas9 activity independent
of gene-specific targeting. As shown in figures (Figure 1- 6, Extended Data Fig. 4), the non-
targeting control sgRNA did not show the phenotypic or base changes observed in the
experimental group, supporting that the observed effects are due to specific gene editing rather
than off-target or AAV-related artifacts. In addition, we also evaluated the bystander editing
efficiency include the non-targeting sgRNA AAV and the off-target effect between non-targeting
sgRNA AAV and targeting sgRNA AAV and we did not observe the bystander editing and off-target
effect caused by non-specific AAV effects (Extended Data Fig. 4).
2. Base Editing Efficiency in Specific Kidney Cell Populations.
The assessment of base editing efficiency is not entirely convincing, as the analysis appears to consider
the whole kidney rather than specific cell types. It is essential to determine whether editing occurs in
epithelial cells, vasculature, or glomeruli. To confirm that editing is occurring in renal tubules, efficiency
should be assessed in isolated tubular cells rather than the entire kidney.
Response: Thanks for your comments and suggestions. As suggested, to determine the editing
efficiency in primary renal tubular cells, we isolated the renal tubules and then tubular cells from
Pkd1RC/RC kidneys injected with Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 particles. We
found that the editing efficiency in renal tubular cells isolated from, 1) Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9
particle injected Pkd1RC/RC kidneys is about 7.21% ± 0.3, similar to that in the whole kidneys (new
Extended Data Fig. 10a), and 2) Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 injected Pkd1RC/RC kidneys was 34.2% ±
8.8 (new Extended Data Fig. 10a), possibly due to the fact that the Ksp promoter is expressed
exclusively in tubular epithelial cells in the kidney but not in other cells (PMID: 10516285).
3. Safety Assessments Following AAV Administration
The study does not adequately address safety concerns related to AAV administration, apart from
measuring renal BUN levels. Liver toxicity is a primary concern with AAV-based therapies; therefore,
assessments of liver function markers (ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin) should be included. Additionally, complete
blood count (CBC) parameters (WBC, RBC, platelet count) should be evaluated to monitor immune
responses. Systemic inflammatory markers such as CRP and cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) should be measured
to assess immune activation. Histological analyses of hepatocyte damage, immune cell infiltration, and
fibrosis should also be performed. Given that high AAV vector doses can induce hepatotoxicity due to
excessive transgene expression, measuring AAV copy number in the liver is critical.
Response: Thanks for your comments and suggestions. We address these concerns point-by-
point below:
1) Liver toxicity is a primary concern with AAV-based therapies; therefore, assessments of liver function
markers (ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin) should be included.
Response: Thanks for your comments and suggestions. We evaluated the liver ALT, AST and
ALP after treatment with Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9. We found that the
levels of ALT, AST and ALP were increased in 3-month old Pkd1RC/RC livers compared to age-
matched wild type livers, while treatment with Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 could decrease the level of
ALT, AST, and ALP to the normal value as in wild type livers(new Extended Data Fig. 11a-11c),
suggesting that treatment with Pkd1 base editors could rescue liver function in Pkd1RC/RC mice.
2) Complete blood count (CBC) parameters (WBC, RBC, platelet count) should be evaluated to monitor
immune responses
Response: Thanks for your comments and suggestions. To evaluate the liver toxicity of base
editors, we detected the levels of white blood cell (WBC), red blood cell (RBC), platelet in blood
of wild type and Pkd1RC/Null mice at PN20 as well as in blood of 3-month-old wild type and
Pkd1RC/RC mice treated with Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 particles. We found
that treatment with high dose Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 or Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 has no significant
effect on the level of WBC, RBC, platelet in the blood from wild type and aged matched Pkd1RC/null
and Pkd1RC/RC mice (new Extended Data Fig. 11d-11i). These results suggested that the doses of
Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 used might not cause immune response in
mice.
3) Systemic inflammatory markers such as CRP and cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) should be measured to assess
immune activation.
Response: Thanks for your comments and suggestions. We evaluated the serum CRP, and
cytokine levels of IL-6, and TNF-α in livers. We found that treatment with high dose Cbh-ABE9-
dual-AAV9 and Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 particles decreased the level of CRP in blood, and IL-6 and
TNF-α in livers in Pkd1RC/RC mice compared to age matched control mice treated with vehicle,
whereas those treatments had no obvious effect on these parameters in wild type mice compared
to age matched wild type mice treated with vehicle (new Extended Data Fig. 11j-11l).
4) Histological analyses of hepatocyte damage, immune cell infiltration, and fibrosis should also be
performed.
Response: Thanks for your comments and suggestions. We performed additional histological
analyses focusing on hepatocyte damage, immune cell infiltration, and liver fibrosis after AAV
treatment in both 3-month and 6-month-old Pkd1RC/RC and WT mice. In brief,
i) for hepatocyte damage, we conducted H&E staining and assessed hepatocyte damage. We
found that there was no massive hepatocyte necrosis in Pkd1RC/RC livers, and only mild structural
disorganization and liver cyst were observed in 3- and 6-month-old Pkd1RC/RC livers (new Figure
5e and 5f), and treatment with Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV particles ameliorated liver cyst in 3- and 6-
month-old Pkd1RC/RC livers, suggesting a protective effect of Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV on
hepatocellular injury in Pkd1RC/RC mice (new Figure 5e and 5f).
ii) for immune cell infiltration, we performed co-immunofluorescence staining for CD45 (pan-
leukocyte marker), CD3 (T cell marker), and CD4 (helper T cell marker) as well as F4/80 in liver
tissues. We found that the numbers of CD3+, CD4+ T and macrophage cells were increased in
Pkd1RC/RC livers compared to age-matched wild-type controls, indicating enhanced immune
infiltration, whereas treatment with either Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 or Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9
decreased the levels of CD3+, CD4+ T cells as well as F4/80 in 3-month-old Pkd1RC/RC livers, and
had no significant effect on those in livers of wild-type controls (new Extended Data Fig. 12 and
new Extended Data Fig. 13). Because the doses of AAV that we used in this study is within the
safety range as reported in previous studies (PMID: 33408413, PMID: 36797478, PMID: 38796705),
these results further indicate that either Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 or Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 treatment leads to the decrease of immune infiltration and early signs of hepatocyte stress
in Pkd1RC/RC livers.
iii) for the evaluation of fibrosis, we performed Masson staining in the livers from 3- and 6-month-
old Pkd1RC/RC and age-matched WT mice treated with Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and Ksp-ABE9-dual-
AAV9. We found that treatment with Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 significantly
decreased fibrosis in 3-month and 6-month-old Pkd1RC/RC and PN20 Pkd1RC/null livers compared
to that in vehicle treated age matched livers (new Extended Data Fig. 19). Together, these results
indicate that Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 treatments leads to the decrease
of immune infiltration, early signs of hepatocyte stress and fibrosis in Pkd1RC/RC livers.
In summary, we did not observe histological signs of hepatotoxicity in H&E-stained liver sections,
further supporting the safety of our AAV treatment regimen. In addition, we have carefully
considered the concern regarding potential hepatotoxicity from high AAV vector doses. In our
study, we used an AAV dosage that is well known within the safety range as reported in previous
studies (PMID: 33408413; PMID: 36797478; PMCID: PMC11286820), none of which reported
liver toxicity at comparable doses.
5) Given that high AAV vector doses can induce hepatotoxicity due to excessive transgene expression,
measuring AAV copy number in the liver is critical.
Response: To assess the safety and persistence of AAV in vivo, we quantified AAV vector
genome copy number and Cas9 protein expression in the liver and kidney at different time points
post-injection. As shown in new Extended Data Fig. 21, the AAV copy number is decreased
kidneys, livers and Cas9 expression were also decreased in kidneys, livers, and hearts of 6-
month-old Pkd1RC/RC mice treated with Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 at PN14. The repaid decrease of
AAV copy number and Cas9 expression in 6-month liver supports a “hit-and-go” gene editing
model, in which Cas9 is briefly expressed to introduce the desired genomic changes and then
cleared gradually, thereby minimizing long-term Cas9 exposure and associated risks. Depending
on the route of administration, choice of serotype and dosage used, the general AAVs (including
AAV9) exhibits a relatively tolerable safety profile when compared to other gene transfer devices
like adenovirus (Ad) and lentivirus (PMID: 33837614). These results indicate that “AAV vector
may not induce hepatotoxicity due to the clearance of AAV and the decreased expression of Cas9,
measuring AAV copy number in the liver is critical.”
4- Influence of Genetic Background on Gene Editing Efficiency
Gene editing efficiency and outcomes can be significantly influenced by the genetic background of the
mouse strain. Differences in DNA repair mechanisms, chromatin accessibility, and immune responses can
contribute to variability in editing efficiency. The authors should consider using an additional mouse
model, such as C57BL/6 (B6) background, to validate their findings in correcting the mutation.
Response: Thanks for your comments. We fully agree that genetic background can influence
gene editing efficiency. The adenine base editors (ABE), which do not rely on double-strand break
formation or the associated NHEJ/HDR DNA repair pathways (PMCID: PMC10586758). The
differences in DNA repair mechanisms are less likely to account for the observed variability in
editing efficiency across mouse strains. However, other strain-dependent factors—such as
chromatin accessibility, promoter activity, AAV transduction efficiency, and immune responses—
can influence editing efficiency.
To determine whether the genetic background of mice affects base editing efficiency, we treated
the C57BL/6 (B6) background Pkd1RC/RC mice with Cbh- and Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 particles, and
found that the editing efficiency was approximately 4.9% and 20.4% (new Extended Data Fig.
10b) in kidneys of the B6 background Pkd1RC/RC mice treated with Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 particle, respectively. These values are lower than those observed in 129
Pkd1RC/RC mice (7.7% for Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and 23.4% for Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9), supporting
the notion that mouse genetic background can affect base editing outcomes.
It has been reported that C57BL/6J miceexisting neutralizing antibodies and increased immune
cell infiltration, which may reduce the effectiveness of AAV-mediated gene therapy (PMCID:
PMC6749937; PMCID: PMC8584150). Furthermore, recent research has demonstrated that
chromatin accessibility differs substantially between C57BL/6J and 129S1/SvImJ mice,
contributing to distinct regulatory landscapes and potentially affecting gene editing outcomes
(PMID: 38153160). These findings reinforce the importance of considering genetic background in
therapeutic gene editing studies and provide validation of our approach in an independent mouse
model.
5- Liver Phenotype:
Given that gene editing via AAV9 is most efficient in the liver, one would expect the most pronounced
phenotypic improvement to occur in this organ. However, in this study, the liver is barely discussed, and
the only provided histological evidence consists of a single low-resolution H&E image. Why is that?
Response: Thanks for your comments. As a proof-of-concept study, we mainly focus on the base
editing in kidneys. We agree that AAV9 is known to transduce the liver with high efficiency, and
we appreciate your comment regarding the expectation of a phenotypic response in the liver. To
address your comment, we have now included additional high-resolution histological analysis of
the liver (new Figure 5e and 5f). Specifically, we performed H&E staining, immune cell infiltration
(CD3, CD4, CD45, and F4/80), and fibrosis analysis in livers in 3-month-old Pkd1RC/RC mice. The
results showed treatment with either Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 or Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 decreases
liver pathology or fibrosis and immune cell infiltration in Pkd1RC/RC mice (new Extended Data Fig.
12 and new Extended Data Fig. 13, new Extended Data Fig. 19).
To better assess the extent of cystogenesis rescue, could you provide full liver section images from Figure
4g? This would offer a more comprehensive view of the overall effect of gene editing on hepatic pathology.
Additionally, biliary abnormalities is more frequently reported than cyst area in the liver in similar models.
It would be valuable for the investigators to analyze and report this aspect as well.
Response: Thank you very much for your comments. We have provided the full liver section
images for new Figure 5e and 5f. To address biliary abnormalities, we performed the masson
staining and analyzed the liver sections with a focus on biliary morphology and found that the
livers from 6-month old Pkd1RC/RC have more massive biliary abnormalities compared to the livers
from 3-month old Pkd1RC/RC and PN20 Pkd1RC/null mice and treatment with either Cbh-ABE9-dual-
AAV9 or Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 particles can decreased fibrosis and biliary abnormalities in
Pkd1RC/RC livers compared to aged matched vehicle group (new Extended Data Fig. 19).
Other comments:
1. H&E Staining Quality: The resolution of H&E staining across all organs is relatively low and not very
convincing. Please provide higher-quality images with both low and high magnification to better visualize
the overall tissue structure and finer details.
Response: Thanks for your comments. We have provided higher-quality images with low
magnification in figure 1-6 and high magnification figures of H&E staining in the new Extended
Data Fig. 2a, new Extended Data Fig. 5a and 5c, new Extended Data Fig. 9a and 9c and new
Extended Data Fig. 14a.
2. Segment-Specific Rescue Analysis: To determine whether gene editing affects specific nephron
segments, could you perform IF staining using segment-specific nephron markers? Suggested markers
include LTL (proximal tubule), NKCC2 (loop of Henle), NCC (distal convoluted tubule), and cytokeratin
(collecting duct).
Response: Thanks for your comments. We have performed the immunofluorescence (IF)
staining
with markers of DBA, LTL, NKCC2, as well as NCC to determine whether gene editing affects the
specific nephron segments in bothAAV9-Cbh-EGFP and AAV9-Ksp-EGFP treated kidneys.
We
found that the GFP signal is mainly co-localized with DBA, LTL, NCC but not with NKCC2,
suggesting that the AAV mediated gene editing mainly affects proximal tubule cells, collecting
ducts cells, distal convoluted tubule but not in loop of Henle (new Extended Data Fig. 1 and new
Extended Data Fig. 7).
3. Serum Creatinine Measurement: Have serum creatinine levels been measured? If so, do they change in
a manner similar to blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels in rescued animals?
Response: Thanks for your comments. We evaluated the serum creatinine levels in 3- and 6-
month-old Pkd1RC/RC and WT as well as PN20 Pkd1RC/null mice and age-matched WT mice treated
with the Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and vehicle control. The new results
showed that treatment with Cbh-ABE9-dual-AAV9 and Ksp-ABE9-dual-AAV9 could decrease
creatinine level in Pkd1RC/RC and PN20 Pkd1RC/null mice compared to aged-match WT (new
Extended Data Fig. 2b, new Extended Data Fig. 5d, new Extended Data Fig. 9b, new Extended
Data Fig. 14b).
4. Western Blot Data Presentation: Since Pkd1 expression in gene-edited animals appears weak, Western
blot data should include all individual data points (three independent samples) run on the same gel, rather
than presenting only a single representative sample.
Response: Thanks for your comments. We have repeated the Western blot data with all individual
data points (three independent samples) run on the same gel and updated the figures in the new
Extended Data Fig. 2j and 2k, new Extended Data Fig. 3a and 3b, new Extended Data Fig. 5b,
5e and 5f, new Extended Data Fig. 9d-9f, new Extended Data Fig. 10c and 10d, and new
Extended Data Fig. 14c.
5. Antibody Validation for PKD1 Detection: Can you confirm the observed Pkd1 upregulation with an
alternative antibody? Several validated antibodies are available from the PKDRRC, which could help
strengthen the findings.
Response: Thanks for your comments. In our study, we used the well-characterized 7e-12
monoclonal antibody developed by Peter Harris’ lab, which has been extensively validated and
widely used in the PKD research field to detect endogenous Polycystin-1 protein (PMID:
25574838). This antibody has demonstrated high specificity and sensitivity in both immunoblotting
with the full length, NTR and NTS of PC1. Given its excellent performance and broad acceptance
in the PKD community, we did not use additional antibody. However, we appreciate the suggestion

6. GFP Expression and Specificity in Extended Fig. 6: The GFP signal driven by the Ksp construct appears

Additionally, co-staining with renal tubule markers is needed to demonstrate colocalization, particularly

Response: Thanks for your comments. We have performed the immunofluorescence (IF)

affects the specific nephron segments in both AAV9-Cbh-EGFP and AAV9-Ksp-EGFP treated

1 and new Extended Data Fig. 7). In addition, we also performed immunohistochemistry staining
and found that GFP is expressed kidneys injected with AAV9-Cbh-EGFP and AAV9-Ksp-EGFP
but not that in kidneys injected with blank AAV (new Extended Data Fig. 8), confirming the
specificity of AAV-mediated GFP expression.
7. Western Blot for PN28 in Fig. 1g: Please include a Western blot for PN28 in Figure 1g.
Response: Thanks for your comments. We have added the Western blot for PN28 in new
Extended Data Fig. 3b.
8. Methodology Details: More details are needed in the Methods section to enhance reproducibility and
clarity.
Response: Thanks for your comments. We have added the details in the Methods section and
highlighted them.
9. Text Clarity and Grammar: The clarity of the text should be improved throughout. For example, in the
abstract, "causing by mutations" should be corrected to "caused by mutations."
Response: Thanks for your comments. We have checked and corrected the grammar errors in
the revised manuscript.
Reviewer #2
In this manuscript, the authors have demonstrated the use of adenine base editing, delivered by adeno-
associated viral (AAV) vectors, to correct a pathogenic variant in the Pkd1 gene that causes kidney and
heart phenotypes (renal cyst growth, cardiac hypertrophy) in mice consistent with human autosomal
dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). They achieve sufficient correction to partially revert the
kidney and heart phenotypes. In a mouse model with exaggerated disease (early mortality), the base
editing is even able to modestly improve lifespan. To my knowledge, this is the first in vivo
demonstration of the use of corrective editing to improve ADPKD and, more generally, any genetic
kidney disease in a mouse model.
The work is technically sound, and I do not have substantive criticisms in that respect. I have the
following suggestions to improve the manuscript.
(1) The authors give themselves more credit than is warranted. "In this study, we developed two adenine
base editors (ABE9) delivered by AAV9" makes it seem like they invented ABE9 for this study, when in
fact it was simply adapted from a publication from another group. "We first developed a broadly
expressed ABE9 base editor system"--they simply swapped out a deaminase domain from ABE8 to ABE9
in existing AAV vectors from another group. "We developed a kidney specific ABE9 base editor system"--
they simply swapped out a promoter from a generally expressed promoter to an established kidney
promoter. From a technical perspective, these are incremental changes. The mouse data are novel
enough on their own to warrant publication--the authors do not need to represent themselves as having
developed whole new technologies. I would advise toning down the language and focusing on what is
truly novel about this work.
Response: Thanks for these comments and suggestions. We appreciate the reviewer’s comment
that “the mouse data are novel enough on their own to warrant publication”. We have revised the
manuscript to tone down the language in multiple sections, including the Abstract, Results, and
Discussion, to more accurately reflect the nature of our contribution. For example, in the revised
abstract, we modified as: “In this study, we adapted one of the gene editing systems, adenine
base editor (ABE9), to develop a broadly and a kidney-specific base editors, and test the effects
of these two systems delivered by AAV9 on preventing disease in humanized Pkd1RC/RC mice
carrying an arginine (R) to cystine (C) mutation that mimics a mutation in ADPKD patients”.
(2) "We developed a kidney specific ABE9 base editor system"--their data plainly demonstrate that it is not
kidney specific, as it produces editing in the liver as well. They did not perform editing biodistribution
studies to assess many organs in the mouse. The major difference they show is that the Ksp promoter
compared to the Cbh promoter reduces expression in the heart. Is this actually a desirable effect, given
that ADPKD causes cardiac hypertrophy, and an optimal ADPKD therapy would target the heart as well as
the kidneys? Are there any meaningful downsides of having corrective editing of Pkd1 to wild-type in
organs other than the kidneys and heart? If not, why is it important to have a kidney specific system? The
authors should better justify this.
Response: Thanks for this thoughtful comment. The rationale for generating both an universal
and a kidney specific base editor is to, 1) determine whether base editor can work in specific
organ, such as kidney, 2) minimize off-target editing and potential toxicity in non-renal tissues,
and 3) explore whether restricting base editing activity to renal epithelial cells can enhance
therapeutic precision compared to universal base editor. Importantly, our results support that
kidney specific base editor works better than the universal base editor in correcting point mutation
in kidney. In addition, our results that kidney specific base editor does not expressed in the heart
support the potential to target specific organs with organ specific base editor in the clinic. Although
kidney specific base editor may avoid off-target effects in non-renal tissues, for that ADPKD is a
systemic disease and cardiac manifestations, such as cardiac hypertrophy, are clinically relevant
(PMCID: PMC7136326), the base editing in other organs—particularly the heart—may not
necessarily be undesirable. The application of universal base editor which can correct mutation
in organs other than kidney may be beneficial in the context of systemic manifestations of ADPKD.
Th liver is a major metabolic and clearance organ that inevitably receives a large proportion of
systemically administered AAV9 vectors. As a result, both universal and kidney specific base
editors can be eventually accumulated in the liver. The certain degree of vector uptake and the
expression of base editor is inevitable, even with tissue-enriched promoters (PMID: 24959122).
This is a known limitation of AAV9 delivery and does not necessarily reflect promoter leakiness
but rather a vector biodistribution. In the revised Discussion, we elaborate on this point.
For the words limitation, we have revised the discussion section as that “With kidney specific base
editor, we intend to, 1) determine whether base editor can work in specific organ, such as kidney,
2) minimize off-target editing and potential toxicity in non-renal tissues, and 3) explore whether
restricting base editing activity to renal epithelial cells can enhance therapeutic precision
compared to universal base editor. Importantly, our results support that kidney specific base editor
works better than the universal base editor in correcting point mutation in kidney. In addition, our
results that kidney specific base editor does not expressed in the heart support the potential to
target specific organs with organ specific base editor in the clinic. We should point out that ADPKD
is a systemic disease with extrarenal manifestations, such as cardiac hypertrophy (PMCID:
PMC7136326) and liver cysts (PMCID: PMC5576944), thus, the application of universal base
editor which can correct mutation in organs other than kidney may be beneficial in the context of
systemic manifestations of ADPKD.”
(3) Can the authors better explain the rationale for using ABE9? In the Discussion section, the authors
imply that ABE8e is ineffective in the kidney (whereas ABE9 is effective), but this is based on studies that
did not focus on the kidney or on kidney-specific genes and so are not that relevant. Furthermore, the
major advantage of ABE9 over ABE8e is that it has less bystander editing without losing much efficiency
(there is no claim of increased efficiency)--or, to put it another way, it has a narrower editing window. But
it is not clear that ABE9 is a better choice than a well-established narrow-window editor like ABE8.8. The
authors do not report any initial screening of ABE9 or other ABEs in cells--this seems odd (and unlikely).
Did the authors really just guess that ABE9 would work the best and go straight to experiments in mice
without any testing in vitro?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. The rationale for choosing ABE9
over ABE8e or other variants is based on the following reasons. First, the target mutation in
Pkd1RC/RC mice lies precisely at position A5 within the protospacer. According to the literature
(PMID: 36229683), ABE9 was specifically engineered to achieve high precision editing at A5 with
minimizing bystander editing at adjacent adenines and cytosines. In fact, ABE9 demonstrates a
highly constrained 1–2 nucleotide editing window centered on A5, with >340-fold higher precision
at this site compared to ABE8e (PMID: 36229683). Second, the broad editing window of ABE8e
(positions A3–A9) and its known off-target cytosine editing make it unsuitable for our disease
model, where specificity is critical. As it has been demonstrated that ABE8e induces substantial
off-target DNA and RNA edits, whereas ABE9 shows background-level off-target activity (PMID:
36229683). Thus, the choose of ABE9 in this study is guided by the editing window required by
our target and by evidence that ABE9 is the most precise editor to date for single-nucleotide A-to-
G conversions, particularly at A5.
For the words limitation, we have revised the discussion section as that “Recently, the ABE7 and
ABE8e systems have been developed and tested in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome and
cardiac disease (PMID: 33408413, PMID: 36797483, PMID: 36634166) However, it has been
reported that ABE7 and ABE8e base editing achieves no obvious editing efficiency in kidneys
(PMID: 33408413). In addition, ABE8e has a broad editing window (positions A3–A9) and a known
off-target cytosine editing (PMCID: PMC7136326). For that the target mutation in Pkd1RC/RC mice
lies precisely at position A5 within the protospacer (Extended Data Fig. 6a), and ABE9 has been
specifically engineered to achieve high precision editing at A5 with minimized bystander editing
at adjacent adenines and cytosines (PMID: 36229683), thus, we adapted the ABE9 system to
generate broad and kidney specific base editors.”
(4) As a proof-of-concept study, the work in this manuscript has considerable merit. However, it seems
unlikely that the dual AAV approach used in this work would advance to the clinic. Indeed, no AAV-based
gene editing therapy has made it very far in the clinic (especially compared to non-viral approaches,
namely lipid nanoparticles), due to the serious downsides of AAV: prolonged expression of the editor
causing a substantial immune response (not typically evident in mice, but quite apparent in large animal
models), along with increased off-target editing; inability to redose the therapy, which is important
because the authors have shown only partial correction of disease in this study, and full correction of the
disease would likely need higher levels of editing that could only be achieved with repeat dosing;
potentially dangerous and even fatal toxicities from having to use high AAV doses in order to (1) account
for the need to use dual AAV vectors to deliver a base editor and (2) get enough vector into the kidneys,
given the broad distribution of AAV9 to many organs throughout the body. The authors should have a
limitations paragraph in the Discussion acknowledging these barriers to translation.
Response: Thanks for this important and thoughtful comment. Actually, the reviewer has already
provided an excellent limitation paragraph. Thank you. We agree that AAV-based delivery
systems—especially dual AAV systems—face significant translational hurdles. While AAV9 was
selected here for its well-characterized in vivo performance and ability to transduce the kidney,
there are alternative delivery platforms—such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs)—are emerging as
more clinically viable options due to their transient expression profile and potential for repeat
dosing (PMID: 34880218, PMCID: PMC10616378). Indeed, the first FDA-approved
investigational new drug (IND) application for in vivo base editing therapy (BEAM-101, targeting
sickle cell disease) employs a non-viral, LNP-based approach, underscoring the clinical
momentum behind such systems (PMCID: PMC9868311). We revised the manuscript to reflect
these limitations as that “While our study demonstrates the feasibility of in vivo adenine base
editing to partially correct Pkd1 mutations in a mouse model of ADPKD, several limitations must
be clarified. First, prolonged expression of Cas9 and the deaminase may increase the risk of off-
target editing and elicit immune responses, particularly in larger animals and humans59, 60.
Second, the use of high AAV doses required for dual-vector delivery to efficiently target kidney
raises safety concerns in both preclinical and clinical settings61. Future efforts are necessary to
develop more compact base editor systems that can be packaged into a single AAV, and non-viral
delivery methods, such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) that are testing in sickle cell disease for
human gene editing applications62. In sum, our current study demonstrates therapeutic potential
and kidney accessibility of base editor, laying the groundwork for further optimization of the
delivery technologies/methods for its clinic potential.”
(5) Line 139: "Both AGA and CGC encode Arg (A)"--this should be "Both AGA and CGC encode Arg (R)".
Response: Thanks for your comments. We have corrected this error in the revised manuscript.
Reviewer #3:
The present manuscript describes a base editing strategy delivered via AAV to correct a mutation in the
PKD1 gene, as a potential therapeutic approach for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
(ADPKD). The authors demonstrate in vivo editing in a mouse model using ABE9 and also engineer a
kidney-specific promoter for targeted AAV expression.
Overall, the manuscript is well-written and supported by comprehensive datasets. The clarity of the
language could be improved by streamlining several sentences that are currently difficult to follow. The
manuscript's structure would also benefit from reorganization for improved data flow (see detailed
comments below). I would recommend the manuscript for publication if authors could sufficiently
address the following concerns:
Major comments:
1. While the authors present robust characterization of editing efficiency and physiological outcomes,
the manuscript lacks any assessment of Cas9-dependent off-target effects. A comprehensive nomination
of potential off-target sites, followed by experimental validation in edited cells or tissues, is critical to
support the therapeutic relevance and safety of the proposed strategy.
Response: Thanks for your comments and suggestions. To address this concern, we predict
potential off-target sites using CRISPOR, a tool ranks the sgRNA with off-target effects and on-
target activity (PMCID: PMC6037314), and then conducted targeted amplicon deep sequencing
(Amplicon-seq). There were no detectable off-target editing above background levels at the top
candidate sites analyzed (new Extended Data Fig. 6g), supporting the high specificity and safety
of the base editing system in vivo.
2. The current structure presents data from AAV injections at PN14 and PN28 (Figures 1 and 2) early in the
Results, while the corresponding editing efficiency data appear later (Figure 4). For improved clarity and
narrative flow, it would be helpful to present the editing outcomes alongside the relevant experimental
context (e.g., incorporating Figure 4 data into Figures 1–3).
Response: Thanks for your comments. We have modified the figures based on this comment by
incorporating Figure 4 data into Figures 1–3.
3. In the Discussion section (Ling 438-444), authors should discuss the limitation of using Ksp promoter
for kidney-specific expression. Since ADPKD also affects other organs, including the heart, the
therapeutic strategy’s limitation in targeting extra-renal tissues should be discussed.
Response: Thanks for the comments and suggestions. We revised the manuscript based on this
comment as: “With kidney specific base editor, we intend to, 1) determine whether base editor
can work in specific organ, such as kidney, 2) minimize off-target editing and potential toxicity in
non-renal tissues, and 3) explore whether restricting base editing activity to renal epithelial cells
can enhance therapeutic precision compared to universal base editor. Importantly, our results
support that kidney specific base editor works better than the universal base editor in correcting
point mutation in kidney. In addition, our results that kidney specific base editor does not
expressed in the heart support the potential to target specific organs with organ specific base
editor in the clinic. We should point out that ADPKD is a systemic disease with extrarenal
manifestations, such as cardiac hypertrophy (PMCID: PMC7136326) and liver cysts (PMCID:
PMC5576944), thus, the application of universal base editor which can correct mutation in organs
other than kidney may be beneficial in the context of systemic manifestations of ADPKD.”
Minor comment:
4. Line 118-120: original ABE paper [PMID: 29160308] should be cited in this sentence.
Response: Thanks for your comments. We have cited this paper in the revised manuscript.
5. Please specify the administration route used for IV injection (e.g., retro-orbital vs. tail vein) in the
Methods section for reproducibility.
Response: Thanks for your comments. We have revised the methods section to clarify this point
as that the administration route used is retro-orbital injection.
6. Figure 1d and other similar plots have both pink and blue dots. What is the difference between the two-
colored dots? Authors should specify in the figure legend.
Response: Thanks for your comments. The two colors represent female (pink) and male mice
(blue), respectively. We clarified this in the revised figure legends.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I still have concerns with the staining data. The IF staining shows markedly more GFP signal in the kidney than in the liver, which is unexpected. Some figures are also unclear—for example, in Fig. 7b, it is not obvious whether the panel represents whole-mount autofluorescence or antibody staining. Additional details are needed for proper interpretation.
Furthermore, the IHC and IF results for GFP are strikingly different. The IF staining suggests transduction efficiencies approaching 90%, which is extraordinarily high for intravenous AAV delivery, whereas the IHC staining shows much lower efficiency (~20%) with an unusual nuclear localization pattern. This discrepancy should be addressed directly. The authors should discuss why their observed kidney transduction efficiency appears unusually high compared with other published studies, and provide possible explanations (e.g., vector dose, construct design, detection sensitivity, or protein uptake artifacts). Additional IHC images of full kidney sections shown side by side with IF images would help clarify this issue.
At present, I remain unconvinced that the GFP signal represents true viral transduction of kidney cells rather than GFP protein synthesized in the liver, released into the bloodstream, and subsequently taken up by renal cells.
Regarding Fig. 21e–f, the vector genome quantification does not convincingly demonstrate cellular transduction. Measuring total AAV DNA in bulk tissue does not prove that the virus actually entered the GFP-positive cells—it could reflect background signal or a minority of infected cells while the GFP protein itself disseminated systemically.
To resolve this, I recommend a straightforward assay such as RNAscope (or intron-spanning RT-qPCR) to directly detect GFP/Cas9 transcripts in kidney, liver, and heart sections. Demonstrating the presence of mRNA within the relevant cells would provide definitive evidence of transcriptional activity, distinguishing genuine transduction from simple protein uptake.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors have satisfactorily addressed my concerns.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors have sufficiently addressed my previous concerns, and the revision has greatly strengthened the manuscript. I have only a few additional minor comments:
• Abstract: The statement that the authors developed “a broadly and a kidney-specific base editors” is inaccurate and potentially misleading. The base editors themselves are not “kidney-specific”; rather, it is the promoters that confer tissue-specific expression. Please revise such phrasing for accuracy for the remainder of the manuscript as well.
• Line 144: Correct “Tada” to “TadA.”

Reviewer #1

Some figures are also unclear—for example, in Fig. 7b, it is not obvious whether the panel represents whole-mount autofluorescence or antibody staining. Additional details are needed for proper interpretation.

the Extended Data Fig. 7b instead of Fig. 7b. In Extended Data Fig. 7b, the images showed the

antibody in the kidney and liver of mice injected with a Ksp-GFP-AAV vector. The GFP signal in
these images was captured by the microscope with the setting of auto-exposure. Thus, the
more or less density of the green signals captured in the whole kidney and liver sections could
not be compared which only represented that the entry of AAV-Ksp-GFP particles and the
expression of GFP in those organs (Extended Data Fig. 7b). We clarified this point in the revised
figure legend of this panel.
Furthermore, the IHC and IF results for GFP are strikingly different. The IF staining suggests
transduction efficiencies approaching 90%, which is extraordinarily high for intravenous AAV
delivery, whereas the IHC staining shows much lower efficiency (~20%) with an unusual nuclear
localization pattern. This discrepancy should be addressed directly. The authors should discuss

published studies, and provide possible explanations (e.g., vector dose, construct design,
detection sensitivity, or protein uptake artifacts). Additional IHC images of full kidney sections
shown side by side with IF images would help clarify this issue.
Response: Thanks for the comments and suggestions. As we response to the concern above,
the GFP auto-fluorescence images but not the IF staining of GFP in Extended Data Fig. 7b were
captured from the whole kidney by the microscope with the setting of auto-exposure, which looked
like the transduction efficiencies were extraordinarily high (about 90% as the reviewer stated).
The appearance of GFP auto-fluorescence in the whole kidney only indicated the entry of Ksp-
GFP-AAV9 particles and the expression of GFP in the kidney but did not represent the
transduction efficiency in kidneys with the injection of Ksp-GFP-AAV9 particles. When we
performed the IF staining with GFP antibody as shown in Extended Data Fig. 7c, we found a
mosaic distribution of GFP epithelial cells within specific nephron segments co-stained with
diverse markers, including DBA, LTL, NCC, NKCC2. With the quantification of the GFP-positive
tubular cells, we found that o⁺nly about 27 % of GFP-positive tubular cells could be detected in the
kidney treated with Ksp-GFP-AAV9 particles. These results indicate that the transduction of AAV-
Ksp-EGFP particles are expressed in specific renal tubular cells in the kidney, which is consistent
with prior reports showing that AAV9 can efficiently target renal tubules, even though those reports
did not quantify the percentages of GFP-positive cells in kidneys (PMID: 37556557, PMCID:
PMC11685967,PMID: 39225099, PMID: 40774951). As suggested, we showed GFP IHC images
side by side with the GFP IF staining in new Extended Data Fig. 7d. The IHC images of the whole
kidney sections were also showed in new Extended Data Fig. 7e.
The nuclear GFP IHC staining might be a technical artifact of the chromogenic IHC procedure,
including chromogen overdevelopment, weak or uneven hematoxylin counterstaining, and the
fixation/antigen retrieval conditions, etc. We repeated the IHC staining with optimized conditions,
including a shorter diaminobenzidine (DAB) development time and an improved nuclear
counterstaining. The new images showed cytoplasmic and membranous GFP staining in tubular
epithelial cells, consistent with the IF staining results (Extended Data Fig. 7d and 7e).
At present, I remain unconvinced that the GFP signal represents true viral transduction of kidney
cells rather than GFP protein synthesized in the liver, released into the bloodstream, and
subsequently taken up by renal cells.
Response: Thanks for the comments. To address this concern, first, we observed that the
distribution pattern of GFP in the images of IF and IHC staining was restricted to renal tubular
epithelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 7c and 7d), rather than a diffuse or vascular pattern that was
usually observed for protein uptake from the circulation. Second, by performing the junction-
spanning RT-qPCR analysis, we confirmed a robust expression of GFP transcript in kidneys
(new Extended Data Fig. 20a-20b), indicating an active transcription of the true viral
transduction of GFP transgene. Together, these results support that the GFP signal reflects true
renal cell transduction and expression, rather than nonspecific uptake of GFP synthesized
elsewhere.
Regarding Fig. 21e–f, the vector genome quantification does not convincingly demonstrate cellular
transduction. Measuring total AAV DNA in bulk tissue does not prove that the virus actually entered
the GFP-positive cells—it could reflect background signal or a minority of infected cells while the
GFP protein itself disseminated systemically. To resolve this, I recommend a straightforward assay
such as RNA scope (or intron-spanning RT-qPCR) to directly detect GFP/Cas9 transcripts in kidney,
liver, and heart sections. Demonstrating the presence of mRNA within the relevant cells would
provide definitive evidence of transcriptional activity, distinguishing genuine transduction from
simple protein uptake.
Response: Thanks for the comments and suggestions. Because our AAV expression cassette

The authors have sufficiently addressed my previous concerns, and the revision has greatly
